messages.content: Hello! Today we are discussing binary search algorithms. To start off, can you explain the main idea behind binary search and what prerequisite is required before we can use it?

Binary search is an efficient search algorithm that works on sorted arrays. The fundamental prerequisite is that the input array must already be sorted in order. The core idea is that we repeatedly divide the search interval in half instead of checking every single element.
Excellent. Walk me through the step-by-step procedure of searching for a target value in a sorted array using indices.

We maintain two pointer indices: low at 0 and high at n - 1. In each step while low <= high, we calculate the middle index mid = low + (high - low) // 2. If array[mid] equals the target, we found our value and return mid.
What happens if array[mid] is not equal to the target?

If target is smaller than array[mid], because the array is sorted, the target must be in the left half, so we update high = mid - 1. Otherwise, if target is larger, we search the right half with low = mid + 1.
Can you analyze the time complexity of this approach compared to simple linear search?

Linear search inspects every element with O(n) time. But in binary search, every comparison reduces the search space by half: n, n/2, n/4, down to 1. That means the worst case takes log2(n) steps, giving O(log n) time complexity. This makes searching massive datasets millions of times faster.
Can you mention one practical edge case when implementing binary search in code?

Got it, that makes complete sense! One important edge case is handling duplicates when we want the first or last occurrence, or handling empty lists. I clearly understand how binary search operates now. Thank you!
